claim: Nineteen subjects between 19 and 33 years of age (mean age 24.5; nine females) participated in the MEG experiment.
source: Nineteen subjects between 19 and 33 years of age (mean age 24.5; nine females) participated in the MEG experiment.
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the Methods section.

claim: One subject was excluded from analysis due to repeatedly falling asleep during the task.
source: We excluded one subject from analysis due to repeatedly falling asleep during the task.
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: The experiment was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (under protocol #14 N-0002).
source: The experiment was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (under protocol #14 N-0002).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: All subjects were right handed and neurologically healthy with normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All subjects were right handed and neurologically healthy with normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: Direct statement about participant inclusion criteria.

claim: All subjects provided written informed consent.
source: All subjects provided written informed consent.
evidence: Direct statement about ethical procedures.

claim: The task was adapted from a previously run fMRI experiment (Wang et al., 2013).
source: The task was adapted from a previously run fMRI experiment (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to prior work.

claim: Two well-known ambiguous images (Necker cube and Rubin face–vase) were used to study bistable perception.
source: In the study, two well-known ambiguous images (Necker cube and Rubin face–vase) were used to study bistable perception under continuous (Ambiguous condition) and intermittent presentation (Discontinuous condition) (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental stimuli.

claim: All face–vase images subtended 16.9 × 17.6 (height × width) degrees of visual angle.
source: All face–vase images subtended 16.9 × 17.6 (height × width) degrees of visual angle, and all cube images subtended 14.3 × 14.5 degree.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus properties.

claim: All cube images subtended 14.3 × 14.5 degrees of visual angle.
source: All face–vase images subtended 16.9 × 17.6 (height × width) degrees of visual angle, and all cube images subtended 14.3 × 14.5 degree.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus properties.

claim: Each subject completed 12 runs, consisting of 4 sets of 3 runs in the following order: Unambiguous, Ambiguous, and Discontinuous conditions.
source: Each subject completed 12 runs, consisting of 4 sets of 3 runs in the following order: Unambiguous, Ambiguous, and Discontinuous conditions.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design.

claim: Each Ambiguous run contained six trials, with each trial consisting of 2 s of written instruction, 2 s of fixation, 60 s of image presentation, and 3–7 s of intertrial interval.
source: Each Ambiguous run contained six trials, with each trial consisting of 2 s of written instruction, 2 s of fixation (while fixating on a crosshair in the center of the screen), 60 s of image presentation, and 3–7 s of intertrial interval (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement about trial structure.

claim: Each ambiguous image was presented three times in a pseudorandom order.
source: Each ambiguous image was presented three times in a pseudorandom order.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus presentation.

claim: Subjects reported every spontaneous perceptual switch using their right hand via one of three buttons throughout the course of image presentation.
source: Subjects reported every spontaneous perceptual switch using their right hand via one of three buttons throughout the course of image presentation: one button for each of the possible percepts, and one for 'Unsure' which they were instructed to press if they experience neither or both of the possible percepts.
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral response method.

claim: Each Unambiguous run contained 32 trials, with each block consisting of 2 s of written instruction, 2 s of fixation, 5 s of image presentation, and 3–7 s of intertrial interval.
source: Each Unambiguous run contained 32 trials, with each block consisting of 2 s of written instruction, 2 s of fixation, 5 s of image presentation, and 3–7 s of intertrial interval (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct statement about trial structure.

claim: The four unambiguous images were presented eight times each in a pseudorandom order.
source: The four unambiguous images were presented eight times each in a pseudorandom order.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus presentation.

claim: Valid trials in the Unambiguous condition consisted of subjects pressing the button for the intended percept once, and no other button presses.
source: Valid trials consisted of subjects pressing the button for the intended percept once, and no other button presses (Figure 1D).
evidence: Direct statement about trial validity criteria.

claim: Each Discontinuous run contained six trials, with each trial consisting of 2 s of written instruction, 2 s of fixation, nine repetitions of 2 s image presentation followed by a 6 s blank period.
source: Each Discontinuous run contained six trials, with each trial consisting of 2 s of written instruction, 2 s of fixation, nine repetitions of 2 s image presentation followed by a 6 s blank period (of which the last second contained the crosshair in the center of the screen) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct statement about trial structure.

claim: The two ambiguous images were presented in alternating trials in the Discontinuous condition.
source: The two ambiguous images were presented in alternating trials.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus presentation order.

claim: Subjects were instructed to fixate upon a crosshair at the center of the screen at all times to avoid the potential influence of gaze on perception.
source: For all conditions, subjects were instructed to fixate upon a crosshair at the center of the screen at all times to avoid the potential influence of gaze on perception.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental instructions.

claim: Response mapping was altered between runs, by switching the buttons for the two percepts.
source: Response mapping was altered between runs, by switching the buttons for the two percepts.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design.

claim: For the first nine subjects the response mapping for the two percepts was switched after every run.
source: For the first nine subjects the response mapping for the two percepts was switched after every run.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental procedure variation.

claim: For the final 10 subjects, the response mapping was switched after every set of 3 runs.
source: For the final 10 subjects, we instead switched the response mapping after every set of 3 runs.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental procedure variation.

claim: Neural activity was recorded using a 275-channel whole-head MEG system (CTF).
source: While performing the task, we recorded neural activity from each subject using a 275-channel whole-head MEG system (CTF).
evidence: Direct statement about recording equipment.

claim: Three dysfunctional sensors were removed from all analyses.
source: Three dysfunctional sensors were removed from all analyses.
evidence: Direct statement about data preprocessing.

claim: Gaze position and pupil size were recorded using a SR Research Eyelink 1000+ system.
source: We also recorded gaze position and pupil size using a SR Research Eyelink 1000+ system.
evidence: Direct statement about additional recording equipment.

claim: Eye-tracking was used for online monitoring of fixation and wakefulness during the experiment.
source: Eye-tracking was used for online monitoring of fixation and wakefulness during the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement about the purpose of eye-tracking.

claim: MEG data were recorded at a sampling rate of 600 Hz, with a low-pass anti-aliasing filter of 150 Hz and no high-pass filter (i.e., DC recording).
source: MEG data were recorded at a sampling rate of 600 Hz, with a low-pass anti-aliasing filter of 150 Hz and no high-pass filter (i.e., DC recording).
evidence: Direct statement about recording parameters.

claim: Before and after each run, the head position of a subject was measured using fiducial coils, in order to detect excessive movement.
source: Before and after each run, the head position of a subject was measured using fiducial coils, in order to detect excessive movement.
evidence: Direct statement about quality control procedures.

claim: All MEG data samples were realigned with respect to the presentation delay of the projector (measured with a photodiode).
source: All MEG data samples were realigned with respect to the presentation delay of the projector (measured with a photodiode).
evidence: Direct statement about data preprocessing.

claim: All preprocessing and analysis of data were performed in MATLAB using custom-written code and the FieldTrip toolbox (Oostenveld et al., 2011).
source: All preprocessing and analysis of data were performed in MATLAB (Mathworks, Natick, MA) using custom-written code and the FieldTrip toolbox (Oostenveld et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement with citation about analysis software.

claim: MEG data were first demeaned and detrended.
source: MEG data were first demeaned and detrended.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing steps.

claim: Data were filtered at 0.05–150 Hz using a third-order Butterworth filter.
source: Data were then filtered at 0.05–150 Hz using a third-order Butterworth filter, and line noise as well as harmonics were removed using fourth-order Butterworth band-stop filters (58–62, 118–122, and 178–182 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement about filtering procedures.

claim: Line noise as well as harmonics were removed using fourth-order Butterworth band-stop filters (58–62, 118–122, and 178–182 Hz).
source: Data were then filtered at 0.05–150 Hz using a third-order Butterworth filter, and line noise as well as harmonics were removed using fourth-order Butterworth band-stop filters (58–62, 118–122, and 178–182 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement about noise removal procedures.

claim: Independent component analysis was applied, and components were manually inspected to remove those related to eye blinks, eye movements, or heart-beat-related artifacts.
source: Independent component analysis (Fieldtrip runica method) was then applied, and components were manually inspected to remove those related to eye blinks, eye movements, or heart-beat-related artifacts.
evidence: Direct statement about artifact removal procedures.

claim: SCP activity was obtained using a third-order low-pass Butterworth filter at 5 Hz.
source: SCP activity was obtained using a third-order low-pass Butterworth filter at 5 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement about feature extraction method.

claim: Alpha-band amplitude was extracted by taking the absolute of the Hilbert transform of the preprocessed MEG data that had been filtered at 8–13 Hz using a third-order Butterworth filter.
source: Alpha-band amplitude was extracted by taking the absolute of the Hilbert transform (Matlab, abs(hilbert(data))) of the preprocessed MEG data that had been filtered at 8–13 Hz using a third-order Butterworth filter.
evidence: Direct statement about feature extraction method.

claim: Beta-band amplitude was extracted by taking the absolute of the Hilbert transform of the preprocessed MEG data that had been filtered at 13–30 Hz using a third-order Butterworth filter.
source: Beta-band amplitude was extracted in the same way, but using data filtered in the 13–30 Hz range.
evidence: Direct statement about feature extraction method.

claim: During the Ambiguous condition, perceptual switching occurred, with group-level results showing that each of the possible percepts was perceived on average >25% of the time.
source: During the Ambiguous condition (Figure 1A, B) perceptual switching occurred, with group-level results showing that each of the possible percepts was perceived (on average >25% of the time), and that subjects were rarely unsure of which percept they were experiencing (<10% occurrence, these time periods were removed from further analyses).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing behavioral results.

claim: Subjects were rarely unsure of which percept they were experiencing (<10% occurrence).
source: During the Ambiguous condition (Figure 1A, B) perceptual switching occurred, with group-level results showing that each of the possible percepts was perceived (on average >25% of the time), and that subjects were rarely unsure of which percept they were experiencing (<10% occurrence, these time periods were removed from further analyses).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing behavioral results.

claim: Time periods when subjects were unsure were removed from further analyses.
source: During the Ambiguous condition (Figure 1A, B) perceptual switching occurred, with group-level results showing that each of the possible percepts was perceived (on average >25% of the time), and that subjects were rarely unsure of which percept they were experiencing (<10% occurrence, these time periods were removed from further analyses).
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion.

claim: Modifying the images to be unambiguous was successful, as evidenced by subjects having on average >80% valid trials.
source: Modifying the images to be unambiguous (Figure 1C, D) was successful, as evidenced by subjects having on average >80% valid trials (defined as trials with only one button press indicating the intended percept).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing behavioral results.

claim: In the Discontinuous condition, there was an increased likelihood that perception remained stable across the blank period for the Necker cube (one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank (17) = 116.5, p = 0.031).
source: In the Discontinuous condition, we found an increased likelihood that perception remained stable across the blank period for the Necker cube (one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank (17) = 116.5, p = 0.031) but not for the Rubin face–vase image (one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank (17) = 71.5, p = 0.736).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results.

claim: In the Discontinuous condition, there was no increased likelihood that perception remained stable across the blank period for the Rubin face–vase image (one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank (17) = 71.5, p = 0.736).
source: In the Discontinuous condition, we found an increased likelihood that perception remained stable across the blank period for the Necker cube (one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank (17) = 116.5, p = 0.031) but not for the Rubin face–vase image (one-tailed Wilcoxon sign-rank (17) = 71.5, p = 0.736).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results.

claim: Perceptual content decoding was performed using a fourfold cross-validated linear support vector machine (SVM).
source: After extracting the relevant neural feature, perceptual content decoding was performed using a fourfold cross-validated linear support vector machine (SVM), with significance determined using cluster-based permutation testing that corrects for multiple comparisons across time.
evidence: Direct statement about analysis method.

claim: Significance of decoding was determined using cluster-based permutation testing that corrects for multiple comparisons across time.
source: After extracting the relevant neural feature, perceptual content decoding was performed using a fourfold cross-validated linear support vector machine (SVM), with significance determined using cluster-based permutation testing that corrects for multiple comparisons across time.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical testing method.

claim: Each subtrial was subsampled by taking 100 equally spaced time points from the beginning to the end of that subtrial.
source: To decode perceptual content, we then subsampled each subtrial by taking 100 equally spaced time points from the beginning to the end of that subtrial (henceforth referred to as percentile of a percept).
evidence: Direct statement about data processing method.

claim: Significant decoding of perceptual content is found for SCP, but not alpha or beta amplitude (except for a very small temporal cluster for the face–vase image).
source: Significant decoding of perceptual content is found for SCP, but not alpha or beta amplitude (except for a very small temporal cluster for the face–vase image), and SCP shows significantly stronger decoding than alpha or beta amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the currently experienced percept is most strongly encoded in SCP activity.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing decoding results.

claim: SCP shows significantly stronger decoding than alpha or beta amplitude.
source: Significant decoding of perceptual content is found for SCP, but not alpha or beta amplitude (except for a very small temporal cluster for the face–vase image), and SCP shows significantly stronger decoding than alpha or beta amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the currently experienced percept is most strongly encoded in SCP activity.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing comparison of decoding results.

claim: The currently experienced percept is most strongly encoded in SCP activity.
source: Significant decoding of perceptual content is found for SCP, but not alpha or beta amplitude (except for a very small temporal cluster for the face–vase image), and SCP shows significantly stronger decoding than alpha or beta amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the currently experienced percept is most strongly encoded in SCP activity.
evidence: Inference based on decoding results showing SCP has strongest decoding accuracy.

claim: These findings are consistent with previous results using other visual perceptual tasks (Baria et al., 2017; Flounders et al., 2019).
source: These findings are consistent with previous results using other visual perceptual tasks (Baria et al., 2017; Flounders et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct statement comparing current results to prior literature.

claim: Broad decoder temporal generalization was observed in the SCP band for both the Necker cube and Rubin face–vase illusion, especially from 20th to 80th percentile of the percept duration.
source: We observed broad decoder temporal generalization in the SCP band for both the Necker cube and Rubin face–vase illusion (Figure 2C, right column), especially from 20th to 80th percentile of the percept duration.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing temporal generalization results.

claim: Neural representation underlying perceptual content, except at the very beginning and end of a percept, is relatively stable over time regardless of percept duration.
source: This suggests that neural representation underlying perceptual content, except at the very beginning and end of a percept, is relatively stable over time regardless of percept duration, and localizes to the SCP band in the frequency domain.
evidence: Inference based on temporal generalization results.

claim: Neural representation underlying perceptual content localizes to the SCP band in the frequency domain.
source: This suggests that neural representation underlying perceptual content, except at the very beginning and end of a percept, is relatively stable over time regardless of percept duration, and localizes to the SCP band in the frequency domain.
evidence: Inference based on decoding and temporal generalization results.

claim: In the Unambiguous condition, significant perceptual content decoding was obtained using SCP activity, but not alpha or beta amplitude (except for one small temporal cluster at image onset for alpha amplitude, face–vase image).
source: Similar to the Ambiguous condition, significant perceptual content decoding was obtained using SCP activity, but not alpha or beta amplitude (except for one small temporal cluster at image onset for alpha amplitude, face–vase image) (Figure 2D, left column) and decoding was stronger in the SCP band (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing decoding results.

claim: Decoding accuracy in the SCP band was highest in the first second after image onset and then drops to a lower level (likely due to neural adaptation).
source: Decoding accuracy in the SCP band was highest in the first second after image onset and then drops to a lower level (likely due to neural adaptation).
evidence: Direct statement with speculative explanation.

claim: The higher decoding accuracy in the Unambiguous condition as compared to the Ambiguous condition is likely due to the differences in sensory input that coincides with different perceptual contents, as well as consistent timing across all trials.
source: The higher decoding accuracy in the Unambiguous condition as compared to the Ambiguous condition is likely due to the differences in sensory input that coincides with different perceptual contents, as well as consistent timing across all trials (all image presentations last 5 s, as opposed to variable percept durations in the Ambiguous condition).
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed difference in decoding accuracy.

claim: The SCP decoder of perceptual content generalized well across time in the Unambiguous condition.
source: Lastly, as in the Ambiguous condition, the SCP decoder of perceptual content generalized well across time in the Unambiguous condition (Figure 2D, right column), suggesting that the underlying neural code is stable over time after the very initial image onset-related activity.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing temporal generalization results.

claim: The underlying neural code for perceptual content is stable over time after the very initial image onset-related activity.
source: Lastly, as in the Ambiguous condition, the SCP decoder of perceptual content generalized well across time in the Unambiguous condition (Figure 2D, right column), suggesting that the underlying neural code is stable over time after the very initial image onset-related activity.
evidence: Inference based on temporal generalization results.

claim: Perceptual content information is decodable from SCP activity, but not from the amplitude of alpha or beta oscillations, regardless of whether sensory input is ambiguous or not.
source: Together, these results show that perceptual content information is decodable from SCP activity, but not from the amplitude of alpha or beta oscillations, regardless of whether sensory input is ambiguous or not.
evidence: Summary statement integrating results from both Ambiguous and Unambiguous conditions.

claim: The state-space analysis aims to identify a neural subspace that is unchanging across time, wherein the trajectory of neural activity informs about changes in behavior across time.
source: Importantly, unlike the decoding approach employed in the earlier analysis, where a different decoder is trained for each time point within a trial and decoder weights are sometimes difficult to interpret (Haufe et al., 2014), the state-space analysis aims to identify a neural subspace that is unchanging across time, wherein the trajectory of neural activity informs about changes in behavior across time.
evidence: Direct statement about the goal of the state-space analysis method.

claim: For the Ambiguous condition, a Type Axis was defined as a binary (0 or 1) variable indicating the current perceptual content.
source: For both the Ambiguous and Discontinuous conditions, we defined a set of behavioral axes capturing both perceptual content and perceptual switching dynamics (Figure 3A). For the Ambiguous condition, these consisted of a Type Axis, which was a binary (0 or 1) variable indicating the current perceptual content; a Duration Axis, indicating the overall duration of the current percept; a Switch Axis, indicating the temporal distance to a reported perceptual switch (i.e., button press); and, finally, a Direction Axis, a binary variable indicating whether the current percept is stabilizing or destabilizing (operationalized as the first half vs. second half of a percept).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral axis definition.

claim: For the Ambiguous condition, a Duration Axis was defined indicating the overall duration of the current percept.
source: For both the Ambiguous and Discontinuous conditions, we defined a set of behavioral axes capturing both perceptual content and perceptual switching dynamics (Figure 3A). For the Ambiguous condition, these consisted of a Type Axis, which was a binary (0 or 1) variable indicating the current perceptual content; a Duration Axis, indicating the overall duration of the current percept; a Switch Axis, indicating the temporal distance to a reported perceptual switch (i.e., button press); and, finally, a Direction Axis, a binary variable indicating whether the current percept is stabilizing or destabilizing (operationalized as the first half vs. second half of a percept).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral axis definition.

claim: For the Ambiguous condition, a Switch Axis was defined indicating the temporal distance to a reported perceptual switch.
source: For both the Ambiguous and Discontinuous conditions, we defined a set of behavioral axes capturing both perceptual content and perceptual switching dynamics (Figure 3A). For the Ambiguous condition, these consisted of a Type Axis, which was a binary (0 or 1) variable indicating the current perceptual content; a Duration Axis, indicating the overall duration of the current percept; a Switch Axis, indicating the temporal distance to a reported perceptual switch (i.e., button press); and, finally, a Direction Axis, a binary variable indicating whether the current percept is stabilizing or destabilizing (operationalized as the first half vs. second half of a percept).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral axis definition.

claim: For the Ambiguous condition, a Direction Axis was defined as a binary variable indicating whether the current percept is stabilizing or destabilizing (operationalized as the first half vs. second half of a percept).
source: For both the Ambiguous and Discontinuous conditions, we defined a set of behavioral axes capturing both perceptual content and perceptual switching dynamics (Figure 3A). For the Ambiguous condition, these consisted of a Type Axis, which was a binary (0 or 1) variable indicating the current perceptual content; a Duration Axis, indicating the overall duration of the current percept; a Switch Axis, indicating the temporal distance to a reported perceptual switch (i.e., button press); and, finally, a Direction Axis, a binary variable indicating whether the current percept is stabilizing or destabilizing (operationalized as the first half vs. second half of a percept).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral axis definition.

claim: Both the Switch and Duration axes had values normalized to the range of [0, 1].
source: Both the Switch and Duration axes had values normalized to the range of [0, 1], such that for the Switch axis, time points corresponding to button presses are 0 and time points furthest away from button presses within each percept are 1; for the Duration axis, the shorted and longest percept durations for a particular subject are coded as 0 and 1, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement about data normalization.

claim: For the Discontinuous condition, only blank periods were analyzed.
source: For the Discontinuous condition, because we are interested in neural activity underlying the perceptual memory trace, only blank periods were analyzed.
evidence: Direct statement about data selection.

claim: For the Discontinuous condition, Pre and Post axes were defined as binary variables indicating the perceptual content before and after the blank period, respectively.
source: Two behavioral axes were defined to capture the content of perception: Pre and Post, which are binary variables indicating the perceptual content before and after the blank period, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral axis definition.

claim: For the Discontinuous condition, a Memory axis was defined as a binary variable indicating whether a perceptual memory trace is present or absent (defined by whether the reported perceptual content before and after the blank period is the same).
source: Two behavioral axes were defined to capture the dynamics of perceptual memory: a Memory axis, which is a binary variable indicating whether a perceptual memory trace is present or absent (defined by whether the reported perceptual content before and after the blank period is the same); and a Blank axis, which is a linearly ramping variable between 0 and 1 from the beginning to the end of each blank period, indicating how long the perceptual memory trace, if present, has last since image offset.
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral axis definition.

claim: For the Discontinuous condition, a Blank axis was defined as a linearly ramping variable between 0 and 1 from the beginning to the end of each blank period, indicating how long the perceptual memory trace, if present, has last since image offset.
source: Two behavioral axes were defined to capture the dynamics of perceptual memory: a Memory axis, which is a binary variable indicating whether a perceptual memory trace is present or absent (defined by whether the reported perceptual content before and after the blank period is the same); and a Blank axis, which is a linearly ramping variable between 0 and 1 from the beginning to the end of each blank period, indicating how long the perceptual memory trace, if present, has last since image offset.
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral axis definition.

claim: Half of the data were used as a training set and a multilinear regression model was fit for each sensor.
source: To extract the neural subspace most relevant to each behavioral metric, half of the data were used as a training set and a multilinear regression model was fit for each sensor (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement about analysis method.

claim: The β weights from the regression model provide an estimate of the relative contributions of the activity of that sensor to each of the different behavioral metrics.
source: The β weights from the regression model provide an estimate of the relative contributions of the activity of that sensor to each of the different behavioral metrics.
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation of regression weights.

claim: The set of weights across sensors for a particular behavioral metric defines the identified neural subspace.
source: The set of weights across sensors for a particular behavioral metric thus defines the identified neural subspace.
evidence: Direct statement about how neural subspace is defined.

claim: For perceptual content ('Type' axis), the neural subspace identified using the SCP activity allows robust prediction of moment-to-moment perceptual content experienced by the subject for the face–vase image.
source: For perceptual content ('Type' axis), we found that the neural subspace identified using the SCP activity allows robust prediction of moment-to-moment perceptual content experienced by the subject for the face–vase image (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Type' column), with highly consistent sensor-level weights across subjects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 'Type' column).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing state-space analysis results.

claim: For perceptual content ('Type' axis), the results did not reach significance for the cube image.
source: Interestingly, the results did not reach significance for the cube image, consistent with weaker perceptual content decoding for the cube than face–vase image (Figure 2A) and potentially due to the decoder being retrained at each time point whereas the subspace is fixed across time points.
evidence: Direct statement with speculative explanation.

claim: Using amplitude of alpha or beta oscillations, perceptual content could not be significantly predicted (except for a small temporal cluster for beta amplitude, cube image).
source: Using amplitude of alpha or beta oscillations, we could not achieve significant prediction of perceptual content (except for a small temporal cluster for beta amplitude, cube image) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Type' column) and there were no consistent weights across subjects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 'Type' column).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing state-space analysis results.

claim: Consistent group-level β weights in occipital cortex for alpha and beta amplitudes were found for the 'Duration' axis, whereby stronger neural oscillations were associated with longer-lasting percepts.
source: Focusing on the 'Duration' axis, which captures variability in the percept durations, we found consistent group-level β weights in occipital cortex for alpha and beta amplitudes, whereby stronger neural oscillations were associated with longer-lasting percepts (Figure 4A, left; reproduced in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 'Duration' column).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing state-space analysis results.

claim: The 'Duration' neural subspace extracted from alpha and beta amplitudes contained significant predictive information for percept durations in the left-out test dataset.
source: The 'Duration' neural subspace extracted from alpha and beta amplitudes contained significant predictive information for percept durations in the left-out test dataset, as evidenced by highly significant correlations between the actual percept duration and predicted percept duration according to neural data collected at different time points during a percept (Figure 4A, right, showing trial-by-trial correlation; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Duration' column, showing predicted percept durations for trials with long vs. short actual percept durations).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing prediction results.

claim: Neural activity related to perceptual stability is relatively persistent across time, evident from the beginning to the end of a percept.
source: These results also show that neural activity related to perceptual stability is relatively persistent across time, evident from the beginning to the end of a percept.
evidence: Inference based on temporal persistence of prediction accuracy.

claim: For SCP activity, significant predictive information over time was found for both images for the 'Duration' axis.
source: For SCP activity, significant predictive information over time was found for both images (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Duration' column); however, there was little consistency between β weights across subjects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 'Duration' column), or between the group-level β weight maps for the two images (cosine similarity, N = 272 sensors, cos θ = 0.08, p = 0.37 assessed by a permutation test).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure and statistical test results.

claim: For SCP activity and the 'Duration' axis, there was little consistency between β weights across subjects.
source: For SCP activity, significant predictive information over time was found for both images (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Duration' column); however, there was little consistency between β weights across subjects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 'Duration' column), or between the group-level β weight maps for the two images (cosine similarity, N = 272 sensors, cos θ = 0.08, p = 0.37 assessed by a permutation test).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure and statistical test results.

claim: For SCP activity and the 'Duration' axis, there was little consistency between the group-level β weight maps for the two images (cosine similarity, N = 272 sensors, cos θ = 0.08, p = 0.37).
source: For SCP activity, significant predictive information over time was found for both images (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Duration' column); however, there was little consistency between β weights across subjects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 'Duration' column), or between the group-level β weight maps for the two images (cosine similarity, N = 272 sensors, cos θ = 0.08, p = 0.37 assessed by a permutation test).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results.

claim: The group-level β weight maps for the 'Duration' axis are highly correlated between the two images for alpha amplitude (cos θ = 0.83, p = 0.02).
source: By contrast, the group-level β weight maps for the 'Duration' axis are highly correlated between the two images for alpha amplitude (cos θ = 0.83, p = 0.02) and beta amplitude (cos θ = 0.82, p = 0.02).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results.

claim: The group-level β weight maps for the 'Duration' axis are highly correlated between the two images for beta amplitude (cos θ = 0.82, p = 0.02).
source: By contrast, the group-level β weight maps for the 'Duration' axis are highly correlated between the two images for alpha amplitude (cos θ = 0.83, p = 0.02) and beta amplitude (cos θ = 0.82, p = 0.02).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results.

claim: Information about perceptual stability, as captured by percept duration, is primarily carried by the amplitude of alpha- and beta-band activity.
source: Therefore, we conclude that information about perceptual stability, as captured by percept duration, is primarily carried by the amplitude of alpha- and beta-band activity.
evidence: Conclusion based on consistency of beta weights across images for alpha and beta but not SCP.

claim: Although information about perceptual stability exists in the SCP band, it is encoded in a less consistent manner across subjects and across different image inputs.
source: Although this information also exists in the SCP band, it is encoded in a less consistent manner across subjects and across different image inputs.
evidence: Conclusion based on lack of consistency in SCP beta weights.

claim: For the 'Switch' and 'Direction' axes, all three neural features were significantly predictive of behavior.
source: For the 'Switch' and 'Direction' axes, we found that all three neural features were significantly predictive of behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Switch' and 'Direction' columns), suggesting that the neural representation of these processes is distributed across multiple frequency bands.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing prediction results.

claim: The neural representation of processes captured by 'Switch' and 'Direction' axes is distributed across multiple frequency bands.
source: For the 'Switch' and 'Direction' axes, we found that all three neural features were significantly predictive of behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, 'Switch' and 'Direction' columns), suggesting that the neural representation of these processes is distributed across multiple frequency bands.
evidence: Inference based on significant prediction across all frequency bands.

claim: For the 'Direction' axis, group-level β weight maps for SCP and beta amplitude show significant sensors lateralized over the left hemisphere whose spatial distribution could be related to the button press response (carried out using the right hand).
source: For the 'Direction' axis, group-level β weight maps for SCP and beta amplitude show significant sensors lateralized over the left hemisphere whose spatial distribution could be related to the button press response (carried out using the right hand).
evidence: Direct statement with speculative interpretation.

claim: For the 'Switch' axis, the SCP-band β weight maps are consistent with a dipole in the midline region corresponding to a potential source in the supplementary motor area.
source: For the 'Switch' axis, the SCP-band β weight maps are consistent with a dipole in the midline region corresponding to a potential source in the supplementary motor area; alpha/beta amplitudes have positive β weights suggesting that the amplitudes decrease around the time of the perceptual switch, consistent with earlier findings (de Jong et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with speculative interpretation and citation to prior work.

claim: For the 'Switch' axis, alpha/beta amplitudes have positive β weights suggesting that the amplitudes decrease around the time of the perceptual switch, consistent with earlier findings (de Jong et al., 2016).
source: For the 'Switch' axis, the SCP-band β weight maps are consistent with a dipole in the midline region corresponding to a potential source in the supplementary motor area; alpha/beta amplitudes have positive β weights suggesting that the amplitudes decrease around the time of the perceptual switch, consistent with earlier findings (de Jong et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to prior work.

claim: For perceptual content reported before and after each blank period ('Pre' and 'Post' axes), only small temporal clusters of significant prediction in the test dataset were found for beta amplitude-defined neural subspace in the case of cube image.
source: For perceptual content reported before and after each blank period ('Pre' and 'Post' axes), we only found small temporal clusters of significant prediction in the test dataset for beta amplitude-defined neural subspace in the case of cube image (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, 'Pre' and 'Post' columns).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing prediction results.

claim: The information contained in neural activity during blank periods about perceptual content experienced earlier or later is weak.
source: Overall, the information contained in neural activity during blank periods about perceptual content experienced earlier or later is weak, which is not surprising, given that there is no active perception related to the cube or face–vase image per se during this period.
evidence: Inference based on weak prediction results with speculative explanation.

claim: All three neural features carried significant information about how far into the blank period the time point was (i.e., the temporal distance to previous image offset).
source: However, all three neural features carried significant information about how far into the blank period the time point was (i.e., the temporal distance to previous image offset), suggesting a strong timing mechanism distributed across frequency bands.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about timing mechanism.

claim: There is a strong timing mechanism distributed across frequency bands during blank periods.
source: However, all three neural features carried significant information about how far into the blank period the time point was (i.e., the temporal distance to previous image offset), suggesting a strong timing mechanism distributed across frequency bands.
evidence: Inference based on significant prediction of elapsed time across all frequency bands.

claim: The SCP topography for the 'Blank' axis shows a midline dipole.
source: The SCP topography shows a midline dipole, and the alpha/beta topographies show widespread sensors whose oscillatory amplitudes decrease as time passes.
evidence: Direct statement about topographic pattern.

claim: The alpha/beta topographies for the 'Blank' axis show widespread sensors whose oscillatory amplitudes decrease as time passes.
source: The SCP topography shows a midline dipole, and the alpha/beta topographies show widespread sensors whose oscillatory amplitudes decrease as time passes.
evidence: Direct statement about topographic pattern.

claim: These results are consistent with previous reports of a contingent negative variation potential (CNV, an SCP activity with generators in the anterior cingulate cortex) and alpha amplitude decreases being neural correlates of temporal anticipation (Nobre and van Ede, 2018).
source: Because the blank periods have a constant duration (6 s) before the next image onset, these results are consistent with previous reports of a contingent negative variation potential (CNV, an SCP activity with generators in the anterior cingulate cortex) and alpha amplitude decreases being neural correlates of temporal anticipation (Nobre and van Ede, 2018).
evidence: Direct statement comparing current results to prior literature.

claim: Significant temporal clusters of prediction in the test dataset were found using alpha and beta amplitudes for the 'Memory' axis, but not SCP activity (which only showed small temporal clusters for the Cube image).
source: Here, we found significant temporal clusters of prediction in the test dataset using alpha and beta amplitudes, but not SCP activity (which only showed small temporal clusters for the Cube image) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, 'Memory' column; alpha and beta results reproduced in Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing prediction results.

claim: The consistency of the group-level β weights across images was stronger for alpha (cos θ = 0.65, p = 0.08) and beta amplitudes (cos θ = 0.75, p = 0.10) than for SCP activity (cos θ = −0.11, p = 0.71) for the 'Memory' axis, although the consistency did not reach significance in any of the neural features.
source: The consistency of the group-level β weights across images was also stronger for alpha (cos θ = 0.65, p = 0.08) and beta amplitudes (cos θ = 0.75, p = 0.10) than for SCP activity (cos θ = −0.11, p = 0.71), although the consistency did not reach significance in any of the neural features.
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results.

claim: The group-level β weight vectors are highly correlated between the Memory axis and the Blank axis for alpha and beta amplitudes.
source: Interestingly, the group-level β weight vectors are highly correlated between the Memory axis and the Blank axis for alpha and beta amplitudes (alpha amplitude: face–vase, cos θ = 0.84, p < 0.01; cube: cos θ = 0.82, p = 0.01; beta amplitude: face–vase, cos θ = 0.83, p = 0.02, cube: cos θ = 0.86, p < 0.01), suggesting a strong timing component to the memory trace.
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test results and inference.

claim: There is a strong timing component to the perceptual memory trace.
source: Interestingly, the group-level β weight vectors are highly correlated between the Memory axis and the Blank axis for alpha and beta amplitudes (alpha amplitude: face–vase, cos θ = 0.84, p < 0.01; cube: cos θ = 0.82, p = 0.01; beta amplitude: face–vase, cos θ = 0.83, p = 0.02, cube: cos θ = 0.86, p < 0.01), suggesting a strong timing component to the memory trace.
evidence: Inference based on correlation between Memory and Blank axis beta weights.

claim: The negative β weights for the oscillation amplitudes show that alpha and beta oscillations are weaker when there is a perceptual memory trace.
source: The negative β weights for the oscillation amplitudes (Figure 4B, left) show that alpha and beta oscillations are weaker when there is a perceptual memory trace.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing beta weights.

claim: The encoding of perceptual memory during the blank periods occurs first in beta activity (at ~0.5–1.5 s after blank onset), followed by alpha activity (at ~1.5–3 s), and is not significant in either frequency band during the latter half of the blank period (3–6 s).
source: Interestingly, the encoding of perceptual memory during the blank periods occurs first in beta activity (at ~0.5–1.5 s after blank onset), followed by alpha activity (at ~1.5–3 s), and is not significant in either frequency band during the latter half of the blank period (3–6 s) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing temporal dynamics.

claim: This transient encoding of perceptual memory in neural dynamics is consistent with a recent EEG study using a similar paradigm (Zhu et al., 2022).
source: This transient encoding of perceptual memory in neural dynamics is consistent with a recent EEG study using a similar paradigm (Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: Direct statement comparing current results to prior literature.

claim: After the transient encoding in beta and alpha activities, perceptual memory trace might be maintained in short-term synaptic plasticity within the network in an 'activity-silent' state without measurable signatures in active neural dynamics (Mongillo et al., 2008; Stokes et al., 2013; Rose et al., 2016).
source: Speculatively, after the transient encoding in beta and alpha activities, perceptual memory trace might be maintained in short-term synaptic plasticity within the network in an 'activity-silent' state without measurable signatures in active neural dynamics (Mongillo et al., 2008; Stokes et al., 2013; Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative statement with citations to prior work.

claim: The neural mechanisms supporting perceptual memory localize to the same frequency bands as those supporting perceptual stability, but have different circuit-level mechanisms.
source: Together with the earlier results showing that stronger alpha/beta amplitudes promote perceptual stability (i.e., longer-lasting percepts) during continuous bistable perception (Figure 4A), these results show that the neural mechanisms supporting perceptual memory localize to the same frequency bands, but have different circuit-level mechanisms.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of results from Ambiguous and Discontinuous conditions.

claim: Sensors supporting perceptual memory (when the stimulus is temporarily removed from view) reside in more anterior regions than those supporting perceptual stability (when the stimulus is in view).
source: In addition, sensors supporting perceptual memory (when the stimulus is temporarily removed from view) reside in more anterior regions than those supporting perceptual stability (when the stimulus is in view) (compare topoplots between Figure 4A, B), suggesting that higher-order brain circuits are recruited to maintain a perceptual memory trace when sensory input is absent, consistent with previous fMRI findings (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures showing topographic differences and citation to prior work.

claim: Higher-order brain circuits are recruited to maintain a perceptual memory trace when sensory input is absent.
source: In addition, sensors supporting perceptual memory (when the stimulus is temporarily removed from view) reside in more anterior regions than those supporting perceptual stability (when the stimulus is in view) (compare topoplots between Figure 4A, B), suggesting that higher-order brain circuits are recruited to maintain a perceptual memory trace when sensory input is absent, consistent with previous fMRI findings (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference based on topographic differences with citation to prior work.

claim: There is evidence that perceptual content is predominantly encoded in the SCP (<5 Hz) range.
source: In this study, we dissected the roles that different types of neural activity play in perception. We found evidence that perceptual content is predominantly encoded in the SCP (<5 Hz) range, and no evidence of perceptual content encoding in the amplitude of alpha and beta oscillations.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding.

claim: There is no evidence of perceptual content encoding in the amplitude of alpha and beta oscillations.
source: In this study, we dissected the roles that different types of neural activity play in perception. We found evidence that perceptual content is predominantly encoded in the SCP (<5 Hz) range, and no evidence of perceptual content encoding in the amplitude of alpha and beta oscillations.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding.

claim: Perceptual content is encoded in the SCP range regardless of whether the sensory input is ambiguous or unambiguous.
source: This was the case regardless of whether the sensory input is ambiguous or unambiguous.
evidence: Summary statement of finding across conditions.

claim: SCP activity along with the amplitude of alpha and beta oscillations encoded aspects of perceptual switching, including the distance to a switch and whether the current percept is stabilizing or destabilizing.
source: We additionally found that SCP activity along with the amplitude of alpha and beta oscillations encoded aspects of perceptual switching, including the distance to a switch and whether the current percept is stabilizing or destabilizing.
evidence: Summary statement of finding.

claim: Information about how long the current percept would last was primarily encoded in alpha and beta amplitudes.
source: However, information about how long the current percept would last and whether a perceptual memory trace would occur if the stimulus is temporally removed from view was primarily encoded in alpha and beta amplitudes.
evidence: Summary statement of finding.

claim: Information about whether a perceptual memory trace would occur if the stimulus is temporally removed from view was primarily encoded in alpha and beta amplitudes.
source: However, information about how long the current percept would last and whether a perceptual memory trace would occur if the stimulus is temporally removed from view was primarily encoded in alpha and beta amplitudes.
evidence: Summary statement of finding.

claim: There is a frequency-band separation of information related to perceptual content and perceptual stability, with the former encoded in raw fluctuations of low-frequency SCP activity, and the latter primarily influenced by the amplitude fluctuations of alpha and beta oscillations.
source: Together, these results show a frequency-band separation of information related to perceptual content and perceptual stability, with the former encoded in raw fluctuations of low-frequency SCP activity, and the latter primarily influenced by the amplitude fluctuations of alpha and beta oscillations.
evidence: Summary statement of main conclusion.

claim: Previous studies on bistable perception have typically focused on one aspect of perceptual behavior at a time, such as perceptual content or perceptual switching.
source: Previous studies on bistable perception have typically focused on one aspect of perceptual behavior at a time, such as perceptual content or perceptual switching.
evidence: Statement about prior research approaches.

claim: By using a novel neural state-space analysis approach, components of neural activity relevant to different aspects of perceptual behavior that all vary across time/trials and are mutually independent can be simultaneously extracted.
source: By using a novel neural state-space analysis approach, we were able to simultaneously extract components of neural activity relevant to different aspects of perceptual behavior that all vary across time/trials and are mutually independent.
evidence: Statement about methodological contribution.

claim: The state-space approach can uncover important relationships between neural activity underlying different aspects of behavior.
source: Additionally, this approach can uncover important relationships between neural activity underlying different aspects of behavior.
evidence: Statement about methodological advantage.

claim: For alpha and beta amplitudes, the state space extracted for 'Blank' and 'Memory' axes in the Discontinuous condition are strongly correlated, suggesting a strong timing mechanism to how perceptual memory is encoded during the blank period.
source: For example, for alpha and beta amplitudes, the state space extracted for 'Blank' and 'Memory' axes in the Discontinuous condition are strongly correlated, suggesting a strong timing mechanism to how perceptual memory is encoded during the blank period (i.e., the neural activity pattern associated with the presence of a perceptual memory trace is similar to the activity pattern that increases over time during the blank period).
evidence: Direct statement with inference about timing mechanism.

claim: The neural activity pattern associated with the presence of a perceptual memory trace is similar to the activity pattern that increases over time during the blank period.
source: For example, for alpha and beta amplitudes, the state space extracted for 'Blank' and 'Memory' axes in the Discontinuous condition are strongly correlated, suggesting a strong timing mechanism to how perceptual memory is encoded during the blank period (i.e., the neural activity pattern associated with the presence of a perceptual memory trace is similar to the activity pattern that increases over time during the blank period).
evidence: Explanation of the inference about timing mechanism.

claim: Compared to multivariate decoding, the state-space method extracts multivariate neural activity patterns relevant to multiple behavioral metrics simultaneously, as opposed to investigating neural correlate of one behavioral metric at a time.
source: Compared to other multivariate analysis methods, the neural state-space method has specific advantages and is well suited to addressing the questions investigated herein. First, compared to multivariate decoding, the state-space method extracts multivariate neural activity patterns relevant to multiple behavioral metrics simultaneously, as opposed to investigating neural correlate of one behavioral metric at a time.
evidence: Statement about methodological advantage.

claim: Compared to automatic dimensionality reduction, such as PCA and similar techniques (Churchland et al., 2012; Cunningham and Yu, 2014; Baria et al., 2017), the state-space approach directly identifies the neural activity pattern (i.e., neural subspace) relevant to a particular behavioral metric, as opposed to being behavior agnostic.
source: Second, compared to automatic dimensionality reduction, such as PCA and similar techniques (Churchland et al., 2012; Cunningham and Yu, 2014; Baria et al., 2017), the state-space approach directly identifies the neural activity pattern (i.e., neural subspace) relevant to a particular behavioral metric, as opposed to being behavior agnostic.
evidence: Statement about methodological advantage with citations.

claim: The finding of perceptual content encoding in the SCP band provides further evidence of the role of SCP in conscious perception, consistent with earlier studies (Li et al., 2014; Baria et al., 2017; Flounders et al., 2019).
source: Our finding of perceptual content encoding in the SCP band provides further evidence of the role of SCP in conscious perception, consistent with earlier studies (Li et al., 2014; Baria et al., 2017; Flounders et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement placing current finding in context of prior literature.

claim: A general role of SCP in supporting conscious awareness (He and Raichle, 2009) is corroborated by recent findings comparing different states of consciousness (Bourdillon et al., 2020; Toker et al., 2022).
source: A general role of SCP in supporting conscious awareness (He and Raichle, 2009) is also corroborated by recent findings comparing different states of consciousness (Bourdillon et al., 2020; Toker et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about broader role of SCP with citations.

claim: Most studies probing neural correlates of perceptual content in bistable perception have employed fMRI (e.g., Tong et al., 1998; Haynes and Rees, 2005; Wang et al., 2013).
source: In the domain of bistable perception, most studies probing neural correlates of perceptual content have employed fMRI (e.g., Tong et al., 1998; Haynes and Rees, 2005; Wang et al., 2013), and most electrophysiological studies have focused on changes in ERPs (e.g., Britz et al., 2009; Pitts et al., 2009), oscillatory power (e.g., de Jong et al., 2016), or neuronal firing rates (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) around perceptual switches.

source: In the domain of bistable perception, most studies probing neural correlates of perceptual content have employed fMRI (e.g., Tong et al., 1998; Haynes and Rees, 2005; Wang et al., 2013), and most electrophysiological studies have focused on changes in ERPs (e.g., Britz et al., 2009; Pitts et al., 2009), oscillatory power (e.g., de Jong et al., 2016), or neuronal firing rates (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) around perceptual switches.

source: Here, by using classic ambiguous figures where the two percepts are symmetrical in salience and level of cortical processing, and showing results consistent across different images, our findings provide a more generalizable electrophysiological correlate of perceptual content.

source: Our results also complement a recent intracranial electrophysiology study using the same ambiguous figures which revealed changes in corticocortical information flow depending on the specific perceptual content experienced (Hardstone et al., 2021).

claim: The potential role of gamma frequency band in encoding perceptual content should be further investigated in future studies using intracranial recordings which are more sensitive to gamma-band activity than MEG (e.g., Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012).
source: Finally, the potential role of gamma frequency band in encoding perceptual content should be further investigated in future studies using intracranial recordings which are more sensitive to gamma-band activity than MEG (e.g., Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012).

claim: A relationship between alpha and beta amplitudes and the stability of percepts has been reported in several previous studies of bistable perception (Kloosterman et al., 2015; Piantoni et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2022).
source: A relationship between alpha and beta amplitudes and the stability of percepts has been reported in several previous studies of bistable perception (Kloosterman et al., 2015; Piantoni et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: Two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms have been proposed for the relationship between alpha/beta amplitudes and perceptual stability: lateral inhibition and the resulting dynamical attractor at a local scale (Piantoni et al., 2017) and top-down feedback from higher-order regions (Kloosterman et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2022).
source: Although the detailed mechanisms involved remain unclear, two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms have been proposed: lateral inhibition and the resulting dynamical attractor at a local scale (Piantoni et al., 2017) and top-down feedback from higher-order regions (Kloosterman et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about proposed mechanisms with citations.

claim: Both local inhibition and top-down processing roles have been ascribed to alpha and beta oscillations (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Michalareas et al., 2016; Spitzer and Haegens, 2017).
source: While both local inhibition and top-down processing roles have been ascribed to alpha and beta oscillations (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Michalareas et al., 2016; Spitzer and Haegens, 2017), we believe that our finding of higher alpha/beta amplitude being associated with stronger perceptual stability (Figure 4A) is more compatible with a top-down interpretation.
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: The finding of higher alpha/beta amplitude being associated with stronger perceptual stability is more compatible with a top-down interpretation.
source: While both local inhibition and top-down processing roles have been ascribed to alpha and beta oscillations (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Michalareas et al., 2016; Spitzer and Haegens, 2017), we believe that our finding of higher alpha/beta amplitude being associated with stronger perceptual stability (Figure 4A) is more compatible with a top-down interpretation.
evidence: Interpretation of current finding.

claim: While lateral inhibition between competing neuronal groups is a key ingredient of biophysical models of bistable perception (e.g., Shpiro et al., 2009), and enhancing cortical inhibition by administering lorazepam, a GABAA receptor agonist, enhances perceptual stability (van Loon et al., 2013), lorazepam also has the effect of reducing alpha power (Lozano-Soldevilla, 2018)—opposite to the present finding of a positive correlation between perceptual stability and alpha power.
source: While lateral inhibition between competing neuronal groups is a key ingredient of biophysical models of bistable perception (e.g., Shpiro et al., 2009), and enhancing cortical inhibition by administering lorazepam, a GABAA receptor agonist, enhances perceptual stability (van Loon et al., 2013), lorazepam also has the effect of reducing alpha power (Lozano-Soldevilla, 2018)—opposite to the present finding of a positive correlation between perceptual stability and alpha power.
evidence: Argument against lateral inhibition interpretation with citations.

claim: Recent intracranial electrophysiological evidence suggests that top-down feedback can carry perceptual templates congruent with long-term priors that act to stabilize a particular percept (Hardstone et al., 2021).
source: By contrast, recent intracranial electrophysiological evidence suggests that top-down feedback can carry perceptual templates congruent with long-term priors that act to stabilize a particular percept (Hardstone et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about prior research with citation.

claim: Given the well-documented role of alpha and beta oscillations in carrying top-down feedback (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Bastos et al., 2015; Michalareas et al., 2016), a plausible mechanism for the present finding of higher alpha/beta amplitudes being associated with longer percept durations is a top-down modulatory influence carried in the alpha and beta bands.
source: Given the well-documented role of alpha and beta oscillations in carrying top-down feedback (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Bastos et al., 2015; Michalareas et al., 2016), a plausible mechanism for the present finding of higher alpha/beta amplitudes being associated with longer percept durations is then a top-down modulatory influence carried in the alpha and beta bands.
evidence: Proposed mechanism with citations.

claim: The finding of alpha and beta amplitudes being associated with perceptual memory is interpreted as reflecting a top-down modulatory influence.
source: Similarly, we interpret our finding of alpha and beta amplitudes being associated with perceptual memory as reflecting a top-down modulatory influence.
evidence: Interpretation of current finding.

claim: A previous fMRI study showed that the content of perception and perceptual memory during intermittent presentation of ambiguous images is especially decodable in higher-order frontoparietal regions, and that intermittent presentation elicits strong top-down influences as compared to continuous presentation (Wang et al., 2013).
source: Consistent with this interpretation, a previous fMRI study showed that the content of perception and perceptual memory during intermittent presentation of ambiguous images is especially decodable in higher-order frontoparietal regions, and that intermittent presentation elicits strong top-down influences as compared to continuous presentation (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about prior research with citation.

claim: The locations of sensors involved in perceptual memory are more anterior than those involved in perceptual stability, which may reflect the source and target of top-down modulation, respectively.
source: The locations of sensors involved in perceptual memory (Figure 4B) are more anterior than those involved in perceptual stability (Figure 4A), which may reflect the source and target of top-down modulation, respectively.
evidence: Interpretation of topographic differences.

claim: The finding of alpha and beta amplitudes being related to perceptual memory is concordant with a recent EEG study (Zhu et al., 2022).
source: Our finding of alpha and beta amplitudes being related to perceptual memory is concordant with a recent EEG study (Zhu et al., 2022), but, superficially, the two studies appear to report opposite directions of this relationship: a negative correlation (manifested as negative β weights) in the present study versus a positive correlation in the earlier EEG study.
evidence: Statement comparing current findings to prior work with citation.

claim: A closer inspection suggests that the present study and Zhu et al. (2022) are in fact consistent: Zhu et al. used short blank durations (~0.5–1.5 s), and alpha/beta amplitudes are higher in stable-blank trials than unstable-blank trials early (within 500 ms of blank-onset) during the blank period, but lower in stable-blank trials (after 800 ms) late in the blank periods.
source: However, a closer inspection suggests that the two studies are in fact consistent: Zhu et al. used short blank durations (~0.5–1.5 s), and alpha/beta amplitudes are higher in stable-blank trials than unstable-blank trials early (within 500 ms of blank-onset) during the blank period, but lower in stable-blank trials (after 800 ms) late in the blank periods (Figure 4B therein).
evidence: Reconciliation of apparent discrepancy with prior work.

claim: The present study used long blank durations (6 s), and the lower alpha/beta amplitude in stable-blank trials is mostly evident at 500 ms following blank onset or later.
source: The present study used long blank durations (6 s), and the lower alpha/beta amplitude in stable-blank trials is mostly evident at 500 ms following blank onset or later (Figure 4B, right, note 'projected average' is amplitude multiplied by β weights, which are negative).
evidence: Statement about current findings.

claim: Both the present study and Zhu et al. (2022) converge to suggest that alpha and beta amplitudes influence not only perceptual stability when sensory input is in view but also perceptual memory when sensory input is temporarily removed from view.
source: The exact neurophysiological mechanisms contributing to these time courses remain to be investigated, but both studies converge to suggest that alpha and beta amplitudes influence not only perceptual stability when sensory input is in view but also perceptual memory when sensory input is temporarily removed from view.
evidence: Summary statement integrating current and prior findings.

claim: The present results differ from previous studies showing beta power increases during working memory maintenance (Spitzer and Haegens, 2017), reinforcing the notion that perceptual memory differs from working memory: the former is unconscious and automatic (Pearson and Brascamp, 2008), while the latter is largely conscious and deliberate (Trübutschek et al., 2019).
source: Importantly, the present results differ from previous studies showing beta power increases during working memory maintenance (Spitzer and Haegens, 2017), reinforcing the notion that perceptual memory differs from working memory: the former is unconscious and automatic (Pearson and Brascamp, 2008), while the latter is largely conscious and deliberate (Trübutschek et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement distinguishing current findings from prior work with citations.

claim: Neural activity (in the alpha and beta bands) underlying perceptual memory has significant overlap with neural activity encoding elapsed time (as evidenced by a significant positive correlation of β weight vectors for the 'Blank' and 'Memory' axes), which fits better with an automatic process as opposed to a working memory account (Souza and Oberauer, 2015; Fulvio and Postle, 2020).
source: Furthermore, we found that neural activity (in the alpha and beta bands) underlying perceptual memory has significant overlap with neural activity encoding elapsed time (as evidenced by a significant positive correlation of β weight vectors for the 'Blank' and 'Memory' axes), which also fits better with an automatic process as opposed to an working memory account (Souza and Oberauer, 2015; Fulvio and Postle, 2020).

claim: Across multiple perceptual conditions (unambiguous vs. ambiguous sensory input; continuous vs. intermittent presentation), distinct components of dynamical neural activity contribute to the content vs. stability of perception.
source: In sum, across multiple perceptual conditions (unambiguous vs. ambiguous sensory input; continuous vs. intermittent presentation), we found that distinct components of dynamical neural activity contribute to the content vs. stability of perception.
evidence: Summary statement of main conclusion.

claim: While perceptual content is encoded in the activity pattern of low-frequency neural activity in the SCP band, perceptual stability and perceptual memory are influenced by the fluctuations of alpha and beta oscillation amplitudes.
source: While perceptual content is encoded in the activity pattern of low-frequency neural activity in the SCP band, perceptual stability and perceptual memory are influenced by the fluctuations of alpha and beta oscillation amplitudes.

claim: These results provide clues to the neural mechanisms underlying stable visual experiences in the natural environment, wherein the ever-present noise and instability in the retinal images must be overcome to reconstruct the cause of sensory input in order to guide adaptive behavior.
source: These results provide clues to the neural mechanisms underlying stable visual experiences in the natural environment, wherein the ever-present noise and instability in the retinal images must be overcome to reconstruct the cause of sensory input in order to guide adaptive behavior.

claim: These results inform future computational models of bistable visual perception and efforts to understand pathological processes underlying perceptual disorders in mental illnesses, including abnormal bistable perceptual dynamics in autism and schizophrenia (Robertson et al., 2013; Kornmeier et al., 2017; Weilnhammer et al., 2020).
source: Finally, these results also inform future computational models of bistable visual perception and efforts to understand pathological processes underlying perceptual disorders in mental illnesses, including abnormal bistable perceptual dynamics in autism and schizophrenia (Robertson et al., 2013; Kornmeier et al., 2017; Weilnhammer et al., 2020).

claim: Studies using frequency-band-specific analysis have shown that the ability to decode perceptual content is contributed most by the slow cortical potential (SCP, <5 Hz) frequency range (Baria et al., 2017; Flounders et al., 2019).
